item.title: Trump’s Retribution Campaign May Face Supreme Court Test
item.description:
Three federal appeals courts have rejected President Trump’s go-to move in trying to install allies as United States attorneys, the officials who lead the prosecutors’ offices in the nation’s 94 judicial districts. In each case, the courts said Trump had violated a law that limits who can run the offices when there are vacancies.

Those decisions have complicated Trump’s efforts to investigate and prosecute his political foes.

The administration this month asked the Supreme Court to review two of the decisions, warning that they “risk chaos” and threaten “to inject mass confusion” into thousands of ordinary cases.

Anne Joseph O’Connell, an expert on the appointment of acting officials at Stanford Law School, said the justices are likely to agree to hear the case. If they do, it could easily turn into a blockbuster ruling on presidential power and again put the court on a collision course with the president.

“I expect that they will take it,” she said, “because it has huge consequences.”

If the court grants review in one or both of the appeals, it is likely to hear arguments in the spring and issue a decision by late June.

The primary question in the cases is whether Trump has complied with a 1998 law, the Federal Vacancies Reform Act. While senior positions in the federal government generally require Senate confirmation, the law sets out some temporary exceptions.

The requirement of Senate confirmation, Alexander Hamilton explained in the Federalist Papers, helps “prevent the appointment of unfit characters” by the president, including those “personally allied to him” and “possessing the necessary insignificance and pliancy to render them the obsequious instruments of his pleasure.”

Still, someone must run the shop after vacancies arise and before a new official is confirmed. That’s where the 1998 law comes in.

It automatically elevates the No. 2 official in the office — the law calls that person the “first assistant” — to be its acting head. If a U.S. attorney quits, gets fired or dies, the existing second-in-command becomes the acting U.S. attorney for 210 days or longer, depending on how confirmation proceedings for the top job play out.

The president can avoid that default provision by picking someone else to run the office, but that person must be presumptively qualified, either by having already been confirmed by the Senate to a different position or by having recently served in a senior role in the relevant office.

Trump has pursued a different alternative. He sought to name a new No. 2 after the vacancy has arisen, arguing that the 1998 law would then convert that official into the acting U.S. attorney.

Trump’s approach would render the alternatives superfluous and invert the statute’s internal logic, Judge Guido Calabresi wrote last month for a divided three-judge panel of the Second Circuit, the federal appeals court based in New York.

“The incentives such a scheme would create run exactly backward,” he added. “An executive who wanted an unqualified loyalist in an acting role would have no reason to use” the alternatives set out in the law, “which demand Senate confirmation or substantial agency tenure.”

The Second Circuit case involved a second issue — the validity of subpoenas issued by a U.S. attorney’s office run by a Trump pick. One of the subpoenas went to the New York attorney general’s office, which Letitia James has led since 2019. They sought, among other things, “any and all documents relating to” a 2022 lawsuit filed by James accusing Trump and his associates of financial fraud.

James, who ranks high on Trump’s enemies list, won the state fraud case at trial, and an appeal is pending. The federal subpoena seeking information about the case was issued by John Sarcone, who was named first assistant long after the vacancy arose and who claimed that meant he had become the acting U.S. attorney.

The Second Circuit disagreed. “Because Sarcone thus lacked any lawful authority to obtain the subpoenas,” Judge Calabresi wrote, “the district court properly quashed them.”

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, last week filed a petition asking the justices to table the Second Circuit case and to grant review of an earlier petition in a case from the Ninth Circuit. It presented the same legal questions, he wrote, but it arose from “a more typical fact pattern” involving run-of-the-mill criminal defendants.

The administration did not seek Supreme Court review of a ruling last year from the Third Circuit, based in Philadelphia, disqualifying Alina Habba, a former personal lawyer for Trump whom he had tried to install as the acting U.S. attorney in New Jersey.

Trump did not invent the idea of naming a first assistant after a vacancy arises and then arguing that the 1998 law automatically elevated that person to be the acting head of the office. Other presidents have done similar things, and often.

“The United States is aware of at least 31 examples at Main Justice alone from the Bush, Obama, Trump and Biden administrations,” the Justice Department told the Second Circuit, referring to its Washington headquarters. “There are doubtless many more examples throughout all executive branch agencies.”

Those appointments were not challenged in court. Judge Calabresi, who was appointed by President Bill Clinton and is a former dean of Yale Law School, said that did not matter. “An executive practice that has gone unchallenged for some time,” he wrote, quoting an earlier decision, “does not, by itself, create power.”

The actions of other administrations proved only, he wrote, “that the original mischief the statute was enacted to curtail persisted, not that Congress blessed it.”

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

Professor O’Connell said Trump’s critics should be careful about what they wished for. Eliminating the president’s ability to install acting officials, particularly after a change in administrations, she said, “would have an asymmetric effect” because an office could be paralyzed if the president is unable to name a new leader whom the Senate would confirm.

“Not being able to have acting officials hurts Democrats more than it hurts Republicans,” she said. “As we’ve seen, Republicans, on average, are willing to let certain agencies not function at all.”

A federal judge ordered the White House to restore the press credentials of journalists at CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

Read the opinion issued early Thursday morning by Judge Timothy Kelly of the U.S. District Court in Washington, who was appointed by Trump.

A state court judge in Iowa dismissed Trump’s lawsuit against The Des Moines Register over a 2024 poll that showed him trailing Kamala Harris, then the vice president.

Read the opinion issued Wednesday by Judge Scott J. Beattie of the Iowa District Court for Polk County. “The First Amendment has its fullest and most urgent application to speech uttered during a campaign for political office,” he wrote.

Mailbag

Why has no one challenged Judge Cannon in Florida, who put under seal Jack Smith’s case against Trump? What are the chances that information will someday be made public? — Dorothy Dortin

Jack Smith, the special counsel who prosecuted Trump between his two terms, dropped the cases after the 2024 election. But Smith prepared a two-volume report on his investigation. The first volume, concerning charges that Trump tried to subvert the 2020 election, was released in January 2025.

Aileen Cannon, a federal trial judge in Florida who was appointed by Trump, has blocked the release of the second volume, which concerned charges that Trump had mishandled classified documents he had retained from his first term.

The history of that second case is tangled. But the important point is that two watchdog groups, the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University and American Oversight, filed appeals to the 11th Circuit, asking it to reverse Judge Cannon’s ruling — and to move quickly. The appeals court granted a motion to put the case on a fast track.

Oral arguments were scheduled for the week of June 22. Then things got weird. Without explanation, the court kicked the arguments to September. Then to the week of Nov. 2. Then to the week of Nov. 16.

Last week, the appeals court canceled that argument, too, and moved it into next year, scheduling it for the week of Jan. 11. On Monday, the court again postponed the argument, now to the week of Jan. 18.

I found this baffling. The 11th Circuit did not respond to an email seeking comment.

Jameel Jaffer, the institute’s executive director, said that he believed something had gone awry — but he wasn’t sure what exactly.

“The appeals court properly recognized the time sensitivity of this case when it ordered Judge Cannon to rule on our motion for access to the report, and it did so again when it granted our request for an expedited appeal,” he said.

“Especially against that background, the delays in scheduling argument are difficult to understand,” he added. “This report addresses allegations of grave criminality by the nation’s highest official. It’s difficult to think of a document whose disclosure to the public could be more important.”

I would love to hear your questions on the law, the courts or whatever is on your mind. Send them my way at the-docket@nytimes.com.

Closing Argument

A federal appeals court judge in Boston had a little fun in an opinion last week. Writing for a unanimous three-judge panel, she rejected an attempt by the winner of $1.35 billion in the Maine State Lottery to sue under a pseudonym.

The opinion was attributed to a Judge Roe.

Then came a footnote: “Just kidding — Judge Thompson authoring here.”

Judge O. Rogeriee Thompson explained in the opinion that her feint was meant to demonstrate the paramount importance of “the principle of transparency as a bulwark of the effectiveness of our judicial system and the public’s trust in it.”

“A creative little formatting tweak in our opening line,” she added, “is an easy thing we can do to remind the public of the historical scaffolding that undergirds our judicial framework of transparency and public access.”

She rejected the lottery-winning plaintiff’s argument that he deserved special treatment given “the unique risks inherent to being an ultra-high-net-worth individual, especially where, as here, the individual’s increase in wealth is swift and drastic.” Among those risks were “kidnap for ransom” and “solicitation for financial support,” said the plaintiff, identified in the opinion as John Doe.

Judge Thompson’s footnote went on for four paragraphs, but it included only two citations for the proposition that the judicial system should err on the side of openness. Both were to the Aug. 27 edition of this newsletter, which bore this headline: “Secrecy in Lawsuits Has ‘Run Amok,’ Scholars Say.” We’re here to serve.

Please send me your comments on retribution, Judge Cannon, pseudonyms or anything else at the-docket@nytimes.com. See you next week. — Adam

item.title: 5 Takeaways From a New Poll on the New Hampshire Senate Race
item.description:
Representative Chris Pappas, a Democrat, leads John E. Sununu, the Republican nominee, by five percentage points in the New Hampshire Senate race, 50 percent to 45 percent, according to a new poll of likely voters conducted by The New York Times and Siena University.

Mr. Pappas’s lead suggests that Democrats retain an advantage in a state where there have been some indicators that Republicans could be competitive even in a favorable environment for Democrats.

The Democratic edge comes despite the two candidates being viewed nearly identically by voters overall, with 43 percent rating Mr. Pappas favorably and 44 percent saying they see him unfavorably. Forty-five percent say they view Mr. Sununu, a former senator, favorably, and 46 percent say they see him unfavorably.

Here are some takeaways from the poll:

Fifty-four percent of voters say they would prefer a Senate candidate who would provide a check on Mr. Trump, compared with 24 percent who would prefer a candidate who supports him. This extends across partisan lines — 11 percent of Republicans say they would prefer a candidate who stands up to Mr. Trump, while less than 1 percent of Democrats say they would prefer a candidate who supports him.

New Hampshire voters prefer Democratic control of the Senate by nine percentage points, 53 percent to 44 percent, but Mr. Pappas leads Mr. Sununu by only five points. Eight percent of voters who want to see Democratic Senate control said they were planning to vote for Mr. Sununu in November.

Mr. Pappas has a wide lead over Mr. Sununu on who would do the best job handling health care and a seven-point advantage on data centers. But the candidates are tied or within a few points of each other on most other issues, including doing what is best for ordinary people in New Hampshire, foreign wars, the cost of living and being an effective senator. Mr. Sununu has an 13-point advantage on supporting American manufacturing.

Nearly 85 percent of Republicans say they are satisfied with their party’s choice of Senate candidate, compared with 75 percent of Democrats. That may reflect a broader difference in how unified each party’s members feel: 56 percent of Democrats and independents who lean toward the Democratic Party say their party is divided, compared with 35 percent of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents. In the Democratic primary, Mr. Pappas defeated a progressive rival who ended up winning nearly 33 percent of the vote.

Nearly 45 percent of voters say “extreme” better describes Mr. Sununu than Mr. Pappas. By comparison, 36 percent say that label better fits Mr. Pappas. On character, the candidates are nearly even: 43 percent say “has good character” better describes Mr. Pappas, compared with 42 percent who say that about Mr. Sununu.

item.title: Weeks Before the Election, Collins’s Ties to a Fund-Raiser Are Under Scrutiny
item.description:
Long before Donald J. Trump upended the Republican Party, Scott Reed was one of its go-to political operatives. He worked on presidential campaigns, ran the Republican National Committee and advised the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, forging mutually beneficial connections across Washington’s political establishment.

One of his closest relationships was with Senator Susan Collins of Maine, and her husband, Tom Daffron, a former Capitol Hill staffer and lobbyist. Mr. Daffron previously worked at Mr. Reed’s government relations firm, and last year it paid him for consulting, according to the senator’s financial disclosure. Mr. Reed has also raised millions of dollars to help Ms. Collins beat back challengers in a Democratic-leaning state and maintain her coveted status as one of the most senior Republicans in the Senate.

The longstanding ties between Mr. Reed and the senator and her husband are now under intense scrutiny following a report by ProPublica that said the F.B.I. had sought to begin a pay-to-play investigation examining Ms. Collins’s interactions with a donor seeking federal contracts. Mr. Reed, who headed a pro-Collins super PAC, exchanged emails with the donor, Martin Kao, according to ProPublica.

The New York Times confirmed that the F.B.I., under the Biden administration, had begun investigating Mr. Kao’s allegations that he and Mr. Reed had discussed circumventing campaign finance laws. Under the Trump administration, F.B.I. officials skeptical of his claims shut down the inquiry last year, The Times reported.

Media coverage of the F.B.I. inquiry arrives at a fraught moment for Ms. Collins, who is currently in the throes of one of the tightest Senate races in the country, one that both parties see as pivotal to control of the chamber. She called the ProPublica article “truly outrageous” and attacked the credibility of Mr. Kao, who is serving an 87-month sentence in federal prison for bank fraud and other charges.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill on Tuesday, Ms. Collins described Mr. Reed as “a person of great integrity.”

Mr. Reed, 66, said he never communicated with Ms. Collins, her staff or Mr. Daffron about Mr. Kao or his company. On Wednesday, he also told The Times that he would continue to raise money for a recently launched super PAC supporting Ms. Collins, Pine Tree Results. The group has spent or reserved $28 million on advertising this campaign cycle, according to AdImpact.

Ms. Collins’s Democratic rival, Troy Jackson, is seizing on the allegations laid out in the ProPublica article as he seeks to pull ahead in the six weeks before the November election.

“The jig is up,” he said in a video on social media. “What Susan Collins just got caught doing is corruption of the highest order.”

Ms. Collins, Mr. Daffron and Mr. Reed all have been fixtures in the Republican establishment for decades, representing the traditional, more moderate wing of the party unwelcome in Mr. Trump’s MAGA movement.

The two men first got to know each other during President Ronald Reagan’s re-election campaign in 1984, Mr. Reed said. A decade later, Mr. Reed met Ms. Collins when she ran, unsuccessfully, for governor of Maine and he was executive director of the Republican National Committee, helping the party sweep Congress in 1994.

Mr. Reed went on to manage Bob Dole’s presidential campaign in 1996. Mr. Daffron led the unsuccessful bid by Mr. Dole’s wife, Elizabeth Dole, for the Republican presidential nomination in 2000. When Mr. Daffron joined Mr. Reed’s lobbying shop, Chesapeake Enterprises, in 2001, Mr. Reed quipped to The Washington Post: “It’ll be one-stop shopping for any Dole memorabilia.”

By then, Ms. Collins was serving her first term in the Senate. Mr. Daffron worked as an executive vice president at Chesapeake Enterprises until 2004, according to Legistorm, which provides information about Capitol Hill.

As Ms. Collins gained seniority in the Senate, Mr. Reed served as the chief political adviser to the powerful U.S. Chamber of Commerce, serving as one of the leading voices for corporate America and steering its congressional endorsements.

“The chamber’s influence greatly increased by having Scott around,” said Charlie Black, a longtime Republican consultant who has known Mr. Reed since the 1980s. “He knew the political landscape and he knew everybody in Washington.”

In 2020, Mr. Reed abruptly left the chamber, citing its endorsements of several Democrats and claiming the organization was insufficiently defending the Republican majority in the Senate. A spokeswoman for the group at the time said Mr. Reed had been pushed out “for cause” and accused him of breaching the organization’s confidentiality rules.

That same year, Mr. Reed leveraged his wide political network to bankroll a super PAC boosting Ms. Collins’s re-election campaign. After she won a tough race against Sara Gideon, the Democratic candidate, Mr. Reed touted Ms. Collins’s refusal to endorse President Trump’s bid for a second term, saying it “reinforced Susan’s independence, that she’s above party politics, that she’s for Maine.”

Two years later, Mr. Kao was indicted on charges of making illegal campaign contributions, and he began to detail a sweeping cash-for-contracts operation on Capitol Hill that involved Ms. Collins and Mr. Reed, according to the ProPublica report. He told federal investigators that Mr. Reed had asked executives of his company for a donation, which he said he was willing to give in exchange for multimillion-dollar defense contracts. As an end run around the law that bans direct contributions by federal contractors, Mr. Kao created a shell company that directed $150,000 to the super PAC led by Mr. Reed, according to ProPublica.

Mr. Reed dismissed his account, saying, “I understand Mr. Kao is now sitting in federal prison.”

Mr. Reed’s profile in Washington has dimmed in recent years, though lobbying records show he still represents several clients on Capitol Hill, including American Airlines and Hillwood Investments, a real estate company based in Dallas.

“He’s not a Trumper, so I don’t hear his name as much anymore,” said Rick Hohlt, a veteran Capitol Hill lobbyist. “He was a huge deal for a long time.”

Mr. Reed has remained close to Ms. Collins and Mr. Daffron. “It’s not an unusual political relationship in Washington, and it’s also a personal friendship,” Mr. Black said.

Mr. Reed’s firm, Chesapeake Enterprises, paid Mr. Daffron more than $1,000 last year, according to the senator’s financial disclosure form. He said that Mr. Daffron, who has served as a chief of staff for three U.S. senators, “has knowledge of the way the U.S. Capitol works second to none.” He continued, “He occasionally helps me guide some of our clients — and never lobbies.”

Mr. Daffron did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Reed’s Pine Tree Results super PAC has raised $20.6 million as of the end of June, records show, largely from out-of-state megadonors. In late July, when Mr. Jackson secured the Democratic nomination, Mr. Reed warned him that he was in for a fight, saying, “We plan to welcome Jackson to the N.F.L. quickly.”

The super PAC has subsequently aired at least five ads attacking Mr. Jackson’s character and his record as a Maine legislator.

item.title: Trump Administration Scrambles to Stop Third-Country Deportations After Court Ruling
item.description:
The Trump administration scrambled on Thursday to halt a number of imminent deportations after an appeals court blocked authorities from expelling people to third countries without a chance to contest their cases, according to documents obtained by The New York Times.

The First Circuit Court of Appeals ruled late Wednesday that starting immediately, migrants need “a meaningful opportunity” to present evidence that they fear deportation to a third country.

Previously, the government had concluded that it could deport the people without such an opportunity by gaining assurances from the nation taking in the migrants that they would not be persecuted or tortured there. This legal interpretation has allowed the administration to sidestep certain processes, such as the fear screening, and rapidly expel people.

The third-country deportation program has been used by the Trump administration to get around rules barring certain people from being deported to their home countries. James Percival, the top lawyer at the Department of Homeland Security, said this week that more than 25,000 people had been deported to third countries.

The program has drawn criticism because many immigrants have been sent to countries with records of human rights violations.

The court decision adds a new burden for the government as it attempts to rapidly remove people from the United States without allowing their lawyers to try to block their deportation.

On Thursday, as news of the ruling spread inside the U.S. government, officials quickly moved to take deportees off flights to third countries such as Costa Rica, Honduras, and the Central African Republic, according to documents obtained by The Times.

The U.S. government has concluded that it cannot move forward — for the time being — with rapid deportations by simply relying on the diplomatic assurances, according to the documents.

Trump administration officials said they would immediately appeal the order.

“Without even allowing the government a chance to respond, and in the dark of night, a federal appeals court blocked us from conducting all third-country removals of illegal aliens, an entirely legal and invaluable tool to stem the tide of illegal immigration,” Todd Blanche, the attorney general, said. “We will immediately seek relief from the Supreme Court, which previously granted a stay in this very same case.”

Mattathias Schwartz contributed reporting.

item.title: Man Killed in Michigan Car Crash Was Not the Target of ICE Search
item.description:
A Guatemalan man who died in a car crash in Michigan after federal immigration agents attempted to question him this week was not the person that agents were looking for, the Department of Homeland Security said on Thursday.

The man who died, Mario David Coronado Juarez, was driving a car registered to the person being targeted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents on Sunday, the agency said in a statement. Mr. Coronado Juarez was a Guatemalan national who was in the United States illegally, the statement said.

According to the agency’s account, ICE agents attempted to stop the car that Mr. Coronado Juarez was driving in the city of Grand Rapids. They were looking for an undocumented immigrant “with multiple alcohol related driving offenses who is also wanted in Guatemala for a drunk and disorderly charge,” according to D.H.S.

At that point, Mr. Coronado Juarez fled at a high speed, the authorities said, and the ICE officers “discontinued the enforcement action.”

Mr. Coronado Juarez, who was the sole occupant of the vehicle, crashed into a tree about a half mile away, the agency said. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Mr. Coronado Juarez had previously been removed from the United States in 2021 and re-entered the country at an unknown date and location, the statement said.

Attempts to reach representatives and family members of Mr. Coronado Juarez on Thursday were not successful.

Gov. Gretchen Whitmer of Michigan, a Democrat, has ordered a state investigation into his death.

The incident in Michigan was the latest in a series of attempted ICE arrests in recent months that have resulted in violence, death and injury, alarming advocates for immigrants who fear that federal agents are intensifying enforcement across the country.

In Austin, Texas, this week, an immigration agent shot an immigrant from Venezuela in his vehicle. That man, Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was hospitalized and then released into ICE custody.

In Evanston, Ill., a suburb of Chicago, a U.S. citizen was left with injuries to his head, neck and teeth after he was mistakenly detained by immigration agents last weekend, according to the local police.

In July, a 28-year-old man running from immigration agents at a gas station in St. Augustine, Fla., was struck and killed by a tractor-trailer. Days before that, an immigration agent in Biddeford, Maine, shot and killed a man in a car. Also in early July, an ICE agent fatally shot a Mexican immigrant, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, during a traffic stop in Houston.

Movimiento Cosecha GR, an advocacy group in Grand Rapids, said in a statement on Wednesday that Mr. Coronado Juarez was 35 and had a wife and children in Guatemala.

“Mario deserves to be remembered not only for the way he died, but for the life he lived: a father, a husband, a brother, and a person deeply loved by his family and his community,” the group said.

Madeleine Ngo contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump and Xi Are Expected to Discuss Accusations of Copying American A.I. Tech
item.description:
One of the more contentious issues President Trump and Mr. Xi are expected to discuss at their summit this week concerns Silicon Valley’s repeated claim that Chinese artificial intelligence companies are maliciously copying advanced American technology.

The big American A.I. labs have long accused Chinese companies, including the tech giant Alibaba, of copying their intellectual property using a technique called “distillation.” The technique allows researchers to collect data from an established A.I. system and use it to build a new system.

Mr. Trump, appearing alongside Mr. Xi at the White House on Thursday morning, listed super intelligence — his preferred term for A.I. — among the “pressing issues” that would be addressed. In a social media post before the meeting, he said it would be a “big topic of discussion” and suggested there would be no change to the way the industry is regulated, despite increasing calls for more government guardrails.

White House officials, however, are expected to confront Mr. Xi over distillation and the copying of American technology, according to recent reports. Chinese companies have never publicly responded to the allegations.

First developed in the early 2010s, distillation was originally a way to build more efficient A.I. systems. Two American A.I. labs, Anthropic and OpenAI, still use distillation in developing their own products. After creating a powerful system like Claude Opus, Anthropic will spend weeks distilling the technology into more efficient systems with names like Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku.

But the labs get annoyed when other companies distill their technologies. Under their terms of service, the two start-ups do not allow outside companies or individuals to distill their most powerful technologies.

After the Chinese start-up DeepSeek shocked American researchers and investors last year by releasing a particularly impressive system, OpenAI accused DeepSeek of distilling its technologies. As Chinese systems continued to improve over the past nine months, Anthropic made several other similar claims.

Some legal experts argue that the practice violates the Defend Trade Secrets Act, which allows companies to sue over the theft of trade secrets. But the courts have not decided this issue.

Copyright law does not necessarily apply because distillation is an effort to copy the behavior of the system, rather than copying it verbatim.
